key_insight: LLMs can absorb incidental details from clinical conversations and background audio, sometimes weaving them into notes or clinical reasoning.
clinical_relevance: For ambient documentation and clinical decision support, systems should be tested for resistance to irrelevant information so they do not record or act on distractions from the encounter.
method: Analyzed 576 patient-clinician dialogues for note generation errors tied to small-talk.
Tested 57 mock consultations with background speech contamination at -10 dB.
Compared frontier and open-weight models on note quality, leakage, and downstream contamination.
evidence_signal: Frontier models inserted small-talk into 35% of notes, with misattribution or clinical use in 3.7%; background speech leaked into 48.2% of transcripts and contaminated 5.3% of downstream notes.
watch_item: Results come from simulated or benchmarked settings, so real-world deployment still needs safeguards that block incidental inputs without harming clinical reasoning.
paper_title: Large language models are vulnerable to incidental information in clinical documentation and reasoning
